subject: Agriculture
title: The Plow Revolution
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Plow Revolution.

hook.text: The steel plow broke the American prairie. Before John Deere's invention, Midwest soil stuck to iron blades.

buildup.text: For millennia, plows were wooden sticks pulled by oxen. Iron plows improved but still couldn't handle sticky prairie soil.

discovery.text: In 1837, John Deere's polished steel plow sliced through prairie like butter. It unlocked millions of acres for farming.

twist.text: Today, no-till farming abandons the plow entirely. The tool that built modern agriculture may be harming it.

climax.text: Plowing destroys soil structure, releases carbon, and causes erosion. No-till preserves soil health and sequesters carbon.

punchline.text: The plow built empires. Now we're learning that not plowing might save them.

quiz.question: Why was John Deere's 1837 steel plow revolutionary?
options: It could cut through sticky prairie soil that defeated iron plows

details.summary: The plow revolution describes how the development of plows—from simple scratch plows to heavy iron moldboards—transformed farming. This topic explains how plowing opened heavy soils to cultivation and enabled the expansion of agriculture across continents.
details.whyItMatters: The plow allowed humans to farm heavier, more fertile soils that were previously impossible to cultivate, leading to population growth and the rise of civilizations.
takeaways: Early scratch plows only worked in light soils of the Mediterranean region
The heavy moldboard plow opened northern Europe's clay-rich soils to farming
Plowing aerates soil and buries weeds but can also accelerate erosion

faq.question: Why was the invention of the plow so important for agriculture?
faq.answer: The plow allowed farmers to break up and turn over heavy soils, bury weeds, and incorporate organic matter. This made fertile but dense land farmable for the first time, dramatically increasing food production.

faq.question: What is the difference between a scratch plow and a moldboard plow?
faq.answer: A scratch plow (ard) simply cuts a shallow groove without turning soil over, suitable only for light soils. A moldboard plow cuts, lifts, and flips a full strip of soil, enabling cultivation of heavy clay-rich ground.
